prompt: A quilter sews a seam connecting the midpoints of two sides of a triangular patch. That seam measures $9$ inches. How many inches long is the third side of the patch — the one the seam does not touch?
hint: A segment joining two midpoints of a triangle is called a midsegment.

hints.text: A segment joining two midpoints of a triangle is called a midsegment.
The Midsegment Theorem: the midsegment is parallel to the third side and exactly HALF its length.
If half the third side is 9, the third side is $2 \times 9 = 18$ inches.

explanation: The seam joins the midpoints of two sides, so it is a midsegment.
By the Midsegment Theorem, a midsegment is half the length of the third side.
The seam is 9 in, so the third side is $2 \times 9 = 18$ in.

alternativeExplanations.title: Which direction to go
steps: Ask which measurement you have: the short one (midsegment) or the long one (third side)?
You have the short one, so you MULTIPLY by 2 rather than divide: $9 \times 2 = 18$ inches.

prompt: A carpenter has bundles of pre-cut boards. Which set of three lengths (in feet) could NOT be joined end to end to form a triangle?
hint: The two shorter boards have to reach across the longest one.

hints.text: The two shorter boards have to reach across the longest one.
Triangle Inequality: the two shorter lengths must add to MORE than the longest.
For choice A, $4 + 5 = 9$, which only equals the longest board — the triangle flattens instead of closing.

explanation: The Triangle Inequality says the sum of any two sides must be GREATER than the third.
Check each set with its two shortest boards: $6 + 8 = 14 > 10$ ✓, $7 + 7 = 14 > 7$ ✓, $5 + 9 = 14 > 12$ ✓.
But $4 + 5 = 9$, which is exactly equal to the longest board, not greater. The two short boards lie flat along the long one and enclose no area, so choice A cannot form a triangle.

alternativeExplanations.title: Try to build it
steps: Lay the 9-ft board down. Hinge the 4-ft and 5-ft boards at each end and swing them up to meet.
They only just touch when both are lying flat on the 9-footer. Lift them at all and they come up short — no triangle.

prompt: A survey stake extends one side of a triangular lot, forming an exterior angle of $(5x)^\circ$. The two remote interior angles measure $(2x + 10)^\circ$ and $(x + 30)^\circ$. Find $x$.
hint: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

hints.text: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
Write $5x = (2x + 10) + (x + 30)$ and combine like terms on the right.

explanation: Check: the exterior angle is $100^\circ$ and the remote interiors are $50^\circ$ and $50^\circ$, which do add to $100$. ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: Verify the whole triangle
steps: With $x = 20$, the two remote interior angles are $50^\circ$ each, and the third angle is the linear-pair partner of the $100^\circ$ exterior angle: $180 - 100 = 80^\circ$.
$50 + 50 + 80 = 180^\circ$, so the lot closes up correctly.

prompt: Two sides of a triangular brace measure $7$ ft and $12$ ft. If the third side must be a whole number of feet, how many different lengths are possible?
hint: The third side has both an upper and a lower limit.

hints.text: The third side has both an upper and a lower limit.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try tiny numbers: with sides $2$ and $3$, the third side satisfies $1 < s < 5$, so $s$ is $2$, $3$ or $4$ — that is $4 - 2 + 1 = 3$ values. Build the range and count the same way with $7$ and $12$.
It must be less than $12 + 7 = 19$ and greater than $12 - 7 = 5$.
Whole numbers strictly between 5 and 19 run from 6 to 18, which is $18 - 6 + 1 = 13$ values.

explanation: The Triangle Inequality gives a range: the third side $s$ satisfies $12 - 7 < s < 12 + 7$, so $5 < s < 19$.
Both endpoints are excluded — at exactly 5 or exactly 19 the triangle flattens into a line.
The whole numbers that fit are $6, 7, 8, \dots, 18$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Count the ends carefully
steps: Counting a run of whole numbers means subtracting and then adding 1, because both ends are included in the run.
From 6 to 18: $18 - 6 = 12$ gaps, but $12 + 1 = 13$ numbers.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap answer is 14, from forgetting the "add 1 at the end" rule or from sneaking 5 or 19 into the list.

Remember the inequality is strict: a side of exactly 19 ft would lie flat along the other two, and a side of exactly 5 ft would too. Neither makes a triangle, so the count runs 6 through 18: 13 lengths.

prompt: A roof truss is the isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}$, so $B$ and $C$ are the base corners. The rafter is extended past $B$, forming an exterior angle at $B$ of $125^\circ$. Find the measure, in degrees, of the vertex angle $\angle A$.
hint: The exterior angle at $B$ and the interior angle $\angle B$ form a linear pair.

hints.text: The exterior angle at $B$ and the interior angle $\angle B$ form a linear pair.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with a friendlier exterior angle: if it were $130^\circ$, then $\angle B = 50^\circ$, $\angle C = 50^\circ$, and $\angle A = 180 - 100 = 80^\circ$. Run those same three steps on $125$.
$\angle B = 180 - 125 = 55^\circ$, and $\angle C$ equals $\angle B$ because the truss is isosceles.

explanation: The exterior angle at $B$ and the interior $\angle B$ sit along a straight rafter: $\angle B = 180 - 125 = 55^\circ$.
Because $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}$, the base angles are congruent, so $\angle C = 55^\circ$ too.

alternativeExplanations.title: Use the Exterior Angle Theorem instead
steps: The exterior angle at $B$ equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, $\angle A + \angle C$, so $\angle A + \angle C = 125^\circ$.
Since $\angle C = 55^\circ$ from the linear pair and the isosceles property, $\angle A = 125 - 55 = 70^\circ$. Same answer, different route.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap is using $125^\circ$ as if it were an interior angle of the truss — that immediately blows the $180^\circ$ budget once you add two base angles.

An exterior angle is always OUTSIDE the triangle. Convert it first with a linear pair ($180 - 125 = 55$), and only then do triangle work. The second trap is stopping at 55, which is a base angle, not the vertex angle asked for.

prompt: Two triangular street signs have two pairs of congruent angles. Which criterion proves the signs are SIMILAR? Answer with two letters.
hint: Count what is known: two angles and no sides.

hints.text: Count what is known: two angles and no sides.
Two angles is enough for similarity, because the third angle comes free from the $180^\circ$ total.
This is AA — Angle-Angle similarity.

explanation: If two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another, the third pair must match too, since all three sum to $180^\circ$.
Matching angles means the same shape, though possibly a different size — that is similarity.

alternativeExplanations.title: Similar vs congruent
steps: Congruence needs at least one side, because sides set the size.
Similarity only cares about shape, so angles alone are enough — which is why AA works for similar but AAA fails for congruent.

prompt: A triangular sail with sides $3$, $4$, and $5$ meters is scaled up for a larger boat to sides $9$, $12$, and $15$ meters. What is the scale factor from the small sail to the large one?
hint: The scale factor tells you what to multiply each small side by.

hints.text: The scale factor tells you what to multiply each small side by.
Divide a large side by its matching small side: $\frac{9}{3}$.
$\frac{9}{3} = 3$, and the other pairs agree.

explanation: The scale factor is the ratio of a new side to its corresponding original side.
Every pair gives the same ratio, so the scale factor is 3 and the sails are similar.

alternativeExplanations.title: Check all three, not just one
steps: A single matching ratio is a hint; three matching ratios is proof of similarity.
Here all three come out to 3, so the big sail is an honest enlargement rather than a stretched-out distortion.

prompt: Two triangular flags satisfy $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$. If $AB = 4$, $DE = 10$, and $BC = 6$, find $EF$.
hint: Similar triangles have proportional corresponding sides. $AB$ pairs with $DE$, and $BC$ pairs with $EF$.

hints.text: Similar triangles have proportional corresponding sides. $AB$ pairs with $DE$, and $BC$ pairs with $EF$.
The scale factor is $\frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5$. Apply it to $BC$.

explanation: The similarity statement pairs $A$ with $D$, $B$ with $E$, and $C$ with $F$, so $\overline{AB}$ pairs with $\overline{DE}$ and $\overline{BC}$ with $\overline{EF}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Set up a proportion
steps: Write $\frac{AB}{DE} = \frac{BC}{EF}$, which is $\frac{4}{10} = \frac{6}{EF}$.
Cross-multiply: $4 \cdot EF = 60$, so $EF = 15$.

prompt: A blueprint shows a scaled-down version of a real bridge truss, so the two figures are similar. Which statement is true about similar figures?

choices.label: Corresponding angles are congruent and corresponding sides are proportional
Corresponding angles are proportional and corresponding sides are congruent
Both corresponding angles and corresponding sides are congruent
Corresponding sides are proportional, but the angles can be anything

hint: Scaling a drawing changes lengths but never tilts the corners.

hints.text: Scaling a drawing changes lengths but never tilts the corners.
Angles stay exactly the same size; sides all shrink by the same ratio.
Angles congruent, sides proportional — choice A.

explanation: Similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size.
Same shape means every pair of corresponding angles is congruent — angles do not scale.
Different size means every pair of corresponding sides is in the same ratio, the scale factor. Choice C describes congruent figures, a special case where the scale factor is 1.

alternativeExplanations.title: Think of a photocopier
steps: Copy a drawing at 50% and every length halves.
But a right angle stays a right angle — no angle is ever "halved" by the copier. That is the whole idea of similarity.

prompt: At the same moment on a sunny afternoon, a $6$-foot-tall student casts a $4$-foot shadow while a flagpole casts a $24$-foot shadow. How tall is the flagpole, in feet?
hint: The sun hits both at the same angle, so the student and the flagpole form similar right triangles.

hints.text: The sun hits both at the same angle, so the student and the flagpole form similar right triangles.
Set up $\frac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}}$ for each: $\frac{6}{4} = \frac{h}{24}$.
Cross-multiply: $4h = 144$, so $h = 36$ feet.

explanation: Both objects stand vertically and the sun's rays arrive at the same angle, so the two right triangles are similar by AA.

alternativeExplanations.title: Use the shadow ratio directly
steps: The student is $6 \div 4 = 1.5$ times as tall as her shadow is long.
Everything standing up at that moment shares the same ratio, so the flagpole is $24 \times 1.5 = 36$ feet tall.

prompt: A $5$-foot mailbox casts a $3$-foot shadow at the same time that a nearby office building casts a $27$-foot shadow. How tall is the building, in feet?
hint: Same sun, same moment: the two right triangles are similar.

hints.text: Same sun, same moment: the two right triangles are similar.
Write $\frac{5}{3} = \frac{h}{27}$.

explanation: The mailbox and the building both stand vertically under the same sun angle, forming similar right triangles.

alternativeExplanations.title: Scale up the shadow
steps: The building's shadow is $27 \div 3 = 9$ times the mailbox's shadow.
Similar figures scale everything by the same factor, so the building is $9 \times 5 = 45$ feet tall.

prompt: Two triangular ramps have two pairs of proportional sides, and the angles BETWEEN those pairs of sides are congruent. Which similarity criterion applies? Answer with three letters.
hint: Read the parts in order around the triangle: side, angle, side.

hints.text: Read the parts in order around the triangle: side, angle, side.
The angle is included between the two proportional sides.
This is SAS similarity.

explanation: The three similarity criteria are AA, SSS (all three pairs of sides proportional), and SAS (two pairs proportional with the included angle congruent).
Here two pairs of sides are proportional and the included angles are congruent, so it is SAS similarity.
Note the difference from SAS congruence: sides here are PROPORTIONAL, not equal — only the angle must actually be congruent.

alternativeExplanations.title: Congruence vs similarity, same letters
steps: SSS and SAS appear on both lists, but with a swap: congruence demands equal sides, similarity only demands a constant ratio.
Angles never scale, so in both versions the angle must be congruent.

prompt: On a surveyor's map, $1$ inch represents $40$ feet of real ground. A property line measures $3.5$ inches on the map. How many feet long is the real property line?
hint: The map and the real lot are similar figures, with a fixed scale factor between them.

hints.text: The map and the real lot are similar figures, with a fixed scale factor between them.
Each inch is worth 40 feet, so multiply: $3.5 \times 40$.
$3.5 \times 40 = 140$ feet.

explanation: A map scale is a scale factor: $1$ inch on paper stands for $40$ feet on the ground.
Set up the proportion $\frac{1 \text{ in}}{40 \text{ ft}} = \frac{3.5 \text{ in}}{x \text{ ft}}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Split the inches
steps: 3 inches represents $3 \times 40 = 120$ feet.
The extra half inch is $0.5 \times 40 = 20$ feet. Together: $120 + 20 = 140$ feet.

prompt: In triangular frame $ABC$, a brace $\overline{DE}$ runs parallel to the base $\overline{BC}$, with $D$ on $\overline{AB}$ and $E$ on $\overline{AC}$. If $AD = 4$, $DB = 6$, and $AE = 6$, find $EC$.
hint: A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides proportionally.

hints.text: A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides proportionally.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try friendly numbers: if $AD = 2$, $DB = 4$ and $AE = 3$, then $\frac{2}{4} = \frac{3}{EC}$ cross-multiplies to $EC = 6$. Build your proportion the same way, top piece over bottom piece on each side.
Set up $\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$, that is $\frac{4}{6} = \frac{6}{EC}$.
Cross-multiply: $4 \cdot EC = 36$, so $EC = 9$.

explanation: Because $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$, the corresponding angles make $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$, and the brace splits the two sides proportionally.
Check the whole sides too: $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{4}{10}$ and $\frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{6}{15}$, and both equal $0.4$. ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: Work with the whole triangles
steps: $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$, so $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AE}{AC}$, that is $\frac{4}{10} = \frac{6}{AC}$.
Cross-multiply: $4 \cdot AC = 60$, so $AC = 15$. Then $EC = AC - AE = 15 - 6 = 9$.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap answer is 15 — writing $\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{AC}$ mixes a PART-to-PART ratio on the left with a PART-to-WHOLE ratio on the right, and lands you on $AC$ instead of $EC$.
Keep both sides of a proportion the same kind: piece-to-piece with piece-to-piece ($\frac{4}{6} = \frac{6}{EC}$), or piece-to-whole with piece-to-whole. Match the types and $EC = 9$ falls out.

prompt: Two similar quilt patches have corresponding sides in the ratio $2 : 3$. The smaller patch has an area of $20$ square inches. What is the area of the larger patch, in square inches?
hint: Areas do not scale by the same ratio that sides do.

hints.text: Areas do not scale by the same ratio that sides do.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: See it on real squares: a $2$ by $2$ square has area $4$ and a $3$ by $3$ square has area $9$ — sides in ratio $2 : 3$ but areas in ratio $4 : 9$. Apply that squared ratio to the $20$.
If sides scale by $\frac{3}{2}$, areas scale by $\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{9}{4}$.
$20 \times \frac{9}{4} = 45$ square inches.

explanation: For similar figures with side ratio $\frac{a}{b}$, the area ratio is $\frac{a^2}{b^2}$ — the scale factor gets squared.
Sides are in ratio $2 : 3$, so areas are in ratio $4 : 9$.
Set up $\frac{20}{A} = \frac{4}{9}$: cross-multiplying gives $4A = 180$, so $A = 45$ square inches.

alternativeExplanations.title: See why it squares
steps: Area involves two dimensions — roughly base times height — and BOTH get multiplied by $\frac{3}{2}$.
So the area is multiplied by $\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{3}{2} = \frac{9}{4}$, and $20 \times \frac{9}{4} = 45$.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap answer is 30, from scaling the area by $\frac{3}{2}$ as if area behaved like a length.
Say it out loud before you compute: "sides scale by $k$, areas by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$." With $k = \frac{3}{2}$, the area factor is $\frac{9}{4}$, giving 45 — not 30.

prompt: A skate ramp is a right triangle: it rises $6$ ft straight up and runs $8$ ft along the ground. How long is the sloped riding surface, in feet?
hint: The two sides that meet at the right angle are the legs; the slope is the hypotenuse. Use $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

hints.text: The two sides that meet at the right angle are the legs; the slope is the hypotenuse. Use $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

explanation: The rise and the run are the legs, so $a = 6$ and $b = 8$.
Take the square root: $c = 10$ ft of riding surface.

alternativeExplanations.title: Spot the family
steps: $6$-$8$-$10$ is just the $3$-$4$-$5$ triple with every side doubled.
Since $3$-$4$-$5$ is a right triangle, so is $6$-$8$-$10$ — the hypotenuse is $10$ with no arithmetic at all.

prompt: A $13$-ft ladder leans against a wall with its foot $5$ ft from the base of the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach, in feet?
hint: The ladder is the hypotenuse — it is the longest side, leaning across from the right angle where wall meets ground.

hints.text: The ladder is the hypotenuse — it is the longest side, leaning across from the right angle where wall meets ground.
Here $c = 13$ and one leg is $5$: solve $5^2 + b^2 = 13^2$.

explanation: The wall and ground form the right angle, so the ladder is the hypotenuse: $c = 13$.
Subtract: $b^2 = 144$, so the ladder reaches $b = 12$ ft up the wall.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why subtract instead of add
steps: When you are hunting the hypotenuse you add the squares; when the hypotenuse is already known you subtract.
Sanity check: $12$ is shorter than the $13$-ft ladder, which is exactly what a leaning ladder should do.

prompt: A carpenter checks corners by measuring three sides. Which set of side lengths makes a **right** triangle?
hint: The converse of the Pythagorean theorem: if $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ then the triangle is right. Test the two short sides against the longest.

hints.text: The converse of the Pythagorean theorem: if $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ then the triangle is right. Test the two short sides against the longest.

explanation: The converse says a triangle is right exactly when the squares of the two shorter sides add to the square of the longest.

alternativeExplanations.title: Carpenters really do this
steps: Builders square up a foundation by measuring $3$ ft along one edge, $4$ ft along the other, and checking that the diagonal is exactly $5$ ft.
Any multiple works, so $9$-$12$-$15$ is the same trick at triple size — handy when the corner is big.

prompt: On a park map, the fountain sits at $(2, 3)$ and the oak tree at $(6, 6)$, where each unit is one meter. How many meters apart are they?
hint: The distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem in disguise: the horizontal gap and vertical gap are the legs.

hints.text: The distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem in disguise: the horizontal gap and vertical gap are the legs.
Horizontal gap: $6 - 2 = 4$. Vertical gap: $6 - 3 = 3$. Now find the hypotenuse.
$d = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ meters.

explanation: Subtract the coordinates to get the legs of a right triangle: $\Delta x = 4$ and $\Delta y = 3$.
$\sqrt{25} = 5$, so the fountain and oak are $5$ m apart.

alternativeExplanations.title: Draw the staircase
steps: From the fountain, walk $4$ m east and then $3$ m north to reach the oak — that path traces two legs of a right triangle.
The straight-line walk is the hypotenuse of that $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle: $5$ m.

prompt: A quilt block is a square $8$ inches on each side. A ribbon is sewn along one diagonal. How long is the ribbon, in inches, rounded to the nearest tenth?
hint: A diagonal cuts the square into two $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles.

hints.text: A diagonal cuts the square into two $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles.
In a $45$-$45$-$90$ triangle the hypotenuse is leg $\times \sqrt{2}$, so the diagonal is $8\sqrt{2}$.
$8\sqrt{2} \approx 8(1.41421) \approx 11.3$ inches.

explanation: The diagonal of a square makes two isosceles right triangles with legs $8$ and $8$.
The $45$-$45$-$90$ shortcut gives hypotenuse $= 8\sqrt{2}$ (the Pythagorean theorem agrees: $\sqrt{64 + 64} = \sqrt{128}$).

alternativeExplanations.title: Estimate first, then trust it
steps: The diagonal must be longer than $8$ but shorter than $8 + 8 = 16$, so somewhere in the low teens.
$\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4$, so about $8(1.4) = 11.2$ — right in that window, which confirms $11.3$ is sensible.

prompt: A $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle has hypotenuse $12$. Write the exact length of the longer leg (the side opposite the $60^\circ$ angle) in simplest radical form.
hint: In a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle the sides go short leg, short leg $\times \sqrt{3}$, short leg $\times 2$.

hints.text: In a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle the sides go short leg, short leg $\times \sqrt{3}$, short leg $\times 2$.
The hypotenuse is twice the short leg, so the short leg is $12 \div 2 = 6$.
The longer leg is $6\sqrt{3}$.

explanation: Find the short leg first: it is always half the hypotenuse, so $12 \div 2 = 6$.
The longer leg is the short leg times $\sqrt{3}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Where the ratio comes from
steps: Fold an equilateral triangle of side $12$ in half — the fold is the height and you get a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle with hypotenuse $12$ and short leg $6$.
The fold line satisfies $6^2 + h^2 = 12^2$, so $h^2 = 108$ and $h = \sqrt{108} = 6\sqrt{3}$.

prompt: A rectangular flag measures $9$ inches by $12$ inches. A gold stripe runs corner to corner. How long is the stripe, in inches?
hint: A diagonal splits the rectangle into two right triangles whose legs are the sides of the rectangle.

hints.text: A diagonal splits the rectangle into two right triangles whose legs are the sides of the rectangle.

explanation: The two sides, $9$ and $12$, are the legs of a right triangle; the stripe is the hypotenuse.
$\sqrt{225} = 15$, so the gold stripe is $15$ inches long.

alternativeExplanations.title: Triple spotting saves time
steps: $9$-$12$-$15$ is the $3$-$4$-$5$ triple scaled by $3$.
Once you recognize the family you can write $15$ immediately and use the squaring only as a check.

prompt: A wheelchair-ramp support is a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle whose hypotenuse is $20$ ft. How long is the side opposite the $30^\circ$ angle?
hint: The side opposite the smallest angle is the shortest side.

hints.text: The side opposite the smallest angle is the shortest side.
In a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle, the hypotenuse is exactly twice the side opposite $30^\circ$.
Half of $20$ is $10$ ft.

explanation: Match each side to its opposite angle: the shortest side faces the $30^\circ$ angle.
The ratio short leg : long leg : hypotenuse is $1 : \sqrt{3} : 2$.
Since the hypotenuse is $20$, the short leg is $20 \div 2 = 10$ ft. Choice A.

alternativeExplanations.title: Reality check the size
steps: Every leg must be shorter than the $20$-ft hypotenuse, which rules out C and D on sight.
Between $10$ and $17.3$, the one facing the *small* angle must be the *small* one: $10$ ft.

prompt: The front of a tent is an isosceles triangle: the two slanted edges are each $13$ ft and the floor is $10$ ft wide. How tall is the tent at its peak, in feet?
hint: Drop the height from the peak straight down to the floor — it splits the isosceles triangle into two identical right triangles.

hints.text: Drop the height from the peak straight down to the floor — it splits the isosceles triangle into two identical right triangles.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up on a $5$-$5$-$6$ triangle: half the base is $3$, so $3^2 + h^2 = 5^2$ gives $h = 4$. Same two moves here — halve the floor width, then use the Pythagorean theorem.
That height hits the middle of the floor, so each small triangle has a leg of $10 \div 2 = 5$ and hypotenuse $13$.

explanation: The height of an isosceles triangle drawn to the base cuts the base exactly in half.
That creates a right triangle with hypotenuse $13$ (the slanted edge) and one leg $5$ (half of $10$).
Solve: $h^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$, so the peak is $h = 12$ ft high.

alternativeExplanations.title: Two triangles, one answer
steps: Both halves are congruent right triangles, so you only need to solve one of them.
Each is a $5$-$12$-$13$ triple — a family worth memorizing alongside $3$-$4$-$5$.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The tempting wrong answer is $\sqrt{169 - 100} = \sqrt{69} \approx 8.3$: using the WHOLE $10$-ft floor as a leg. But the full floor is not a leg of either right triangle — the height lands in the middle of it.
Before squaring anything, redraw the picture with the height in place and label the halved base. Half of $10$ is $5$, and $13^2 - 5^2$ gives the clean $12$.

prompt: On a coordinate grid a drone flies straight from $(-3, 2)$ to $(5, -4)$. How far does it fly, in units?
hint: Find the horizontal gap and the vertical gap first — subtracting a negative is the same as adding.

hints.text: Find the horizontal gap and the vertical gap first — subtracting a negative is the same as adding.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try an easy pair first: from $(0, 0)$ to $(3, 4)$ the gaps are $3$ and $4$, so $d = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$. Your points only need one subtraction each to find those gaps.
$\Delta x = 5 - (-3) = 8$ and $\Delta y = -4 - 2 = -6$. Squaring kills the minus sign.

explanation: The distance formula squares both, so the sign of $-6$ does not matter: $64 + 36 = 100$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Count it on the grid
steps: From $(-3, 2)$, walk $8$ units right and $6$ units down to land on $(5, -4)$.
Those legs make an $8$-$6$-$10$ right triangle (the $3$-$4$-$5$ triple doubled), so the straight flight is $10$ units.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice C, $100$, is the answer of someone who stopped one keystroke early — $8^2 + 6^2 = 100$ is $d^2$, not $d$. Choice B, $14$, comes from adding the legs $8 + 6$ instead of using the triangle.
Write the formula with the square root symbol already on the page, then fill it in. The last thing you do is take the root: $\sqrt{100} = 10$.

prompt: In right triangle $ABC$ the right angle is at $C$. The side opposite $\angle A$ is $3$ and the hypotenuse is $5$. What is $\sin A$? Give a decimal.
hint: SOH: **S**ine is **O**pposite over **H**ypotenuse.

hints.text: SOH: **S**ine is **O**pposite over **H**ypotenuse.
Opposite $\angle A$ is $3$; the hypotenuse is $5$. Divide.

explanation: Sine of an angle is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why it is always less than 1
steps: The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle, so the opposite side is always smaller.
A smaller number over a bigger one is less than $1$ — if your sine ever comes out above $1$, you flipped the fraction.

prompt: In a right triangle, the side adjacent to $\angle P$ measures $24$ and the hypotenuse measures $25$. What is $\cos P$? Give a decimal.
hint: CAH: **C**osine is **A**djacent over **H**ypotenuse.

hints.text: CAH: **C**osine is **A**djacent over **H**ypotenuse.
Adjacent is $24$, hypotenuse is $25$, so $\cos P = \frac{24}{25}$.

explanation: Cosine is the adjacent leg over the hypotenuse.

alternativeExplanations.title: What 0.96 tells you
steps: A cosine that close to $1$ means the adjacent leg is nearly as long as the hypotenuse.
That happens when the angle is small and skinny — this angle is only about $16^\circ$.

prompt: You know one acute angle of a right triangle and the length of the hypotenuse, and you want the leg **adjacent** to that angle. Which ratio should you use?

choices.label: The Pythagorean theorem — trigonometry cannot help here

hint: List the two sides in play: the one you want (adjacent) and the one you know (hypotenuse).

hints.text: List the two sides in play: the one you want (adjacent) and the one you know (hypotenuse).
Which of the three ratios connects exactly adjacent and hypotenuse?
Cosine — CAH. Choice B.

explanation: Pick the ratio by which two sides are involved, never by habit.
Adjacent plus hypotenuse is the cosine pair (CAH).
Tangent needs the opposite side, which you do not know, and the Pythagorean theorem needs two sides, not an angle. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: A two-second routine
steps: Mark the angle, then label the three sides: opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse.
Circle the side you know and the side you want; the two circles pick the ratio for you every single time.

prompt: A loading ramp is $15$ ft long and rises at an angle of $20^\circ$ to the ground. How high is the top of the ramp above the ground, in feet, rounded to the nearest tenth?
hint: The ramp itself is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the $20^\circ$ angle.

hints.text: The ramp itself is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the $20^\circ$ angle.
Opposite and hypotenuse means sine: $\sin 20^\circ = \frac{h}{15}$.
$h = 15 \sin 20^\circ \approx 15(0.342) \approx 5.1$ ft.

explanation: Label the triangle: hypotenuse $= 15$ (the ramp), unknown height opposite the $20^\circ$ angle.
Opposite over hypotenuse is sine, so $\sin 20^\circ = \frac{h}{15}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Does the size make sense?
steps: A shallow $20^\circ$ climb should gain only a little height over $15$ ft of travel.
About $5$ ft of rise for $15$ ft of ramp feels right; an answer like $14$ ft would mean a nearly vertical ramp.

prompt: A flagpole is $30$ ft tall and casts a shadow $40$ ft long on level ground. What is the angle of elevation of the sun, in degrees, rounded to the nearest tenth?
hint: You know both legs — the pole (opposite) and the shadow (adjacent) — so use tangent.

hints.text: You know both legs — the pole (opposite) and the shadow (adjacent) — so use tangent.
$\tan \theta = \frac{30}{40} = 0.75$. To undo tangent, use $\tan^{-1}$.
$\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 36.9^\circ$.

explanation: The sun's angle of elevation sits at the tip of the shadow, between the ground and the ray to the top of the pole.

alternativeExplanations.title: Estimate before you press buttons
steps: The shadow is longer than the pole, so the angle must be less than $45^\circ$ (at exactly $45^\circ$ they would be equal).
$36.9^\circ$ passes that check; anything above $45^\circ$ would mean you flipped the fraction.

prompt: From the top of a $120$-ft lighthouse, the angle of depression to a sailboat is $25^\circ$. How far is the boat from the base of the lighthouse, in feet, rounded to the nearest tenth?
hint: The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the boat — they are alternate interior angles across the horizontal.

hints.text: The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the boat — they are alternate interior angles across the horizontal.
From the boat's corner, the lighthouse ($120$) is opposite and the water distance $d$ is adjacent: $\tan 25^\circ = \frac{120}{d}$.
$d = \frac{120}{\tan 25^\circ} \approx \frac{120}{0.4663} \approx 257.3$ ft.

explanation: Slide the $25^\circ$ angle of depression down to the boat — it becomes a $25^\circ$ angle of elevation inside the triangle.
With that angle, the height $120$ is opposite and the distance $d$ is adjacent, so $\tan 25^\circ = \frac{120}{d}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: A shallow angle means a far boat
steps: Looking down only $25^\circ$ from a $120$-ft tower means the boat is well out to sea.
The answer, over $250$ ft, is more than twice the tower height — exactly what a shallow sight line should give.

prompt: A kite is flying on $80$ ft of taut string that makes a $40^\circ$ angle with the level ground. Which calculation gives the kite's height above the ground?
hint: The string is the hypotenuse; the height is the side opposite the $40^\circ$ angle.

hints.text: The string is the hypotenuse; the height is the side opposite the $40^\circ$ angle.
Opposite and hypotenuse means sine: $\sin 40^\circ = \frac{h}{80}$.
Multiply: $h = 80 \sin 40^\circ \approx 51.4$ ft. Choice A.

explanation: The taut string is the longest side of the triangle, so it is the hypotenuse: $80$ ft.
Height is opposite the $40^\circ$ angle, and opposite-over-hypotenuse is sine: $\sin 40^\circ = \frac{h}{80}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Eliminate the impossible
steps: The height can never exceed the $80$ ft of string, so choice D is out before any arithmetic.
Choice B is the horizontal distance and C uses the wrong pair of sides entirely — only A pairs the height with the hypotenuse.

prompt: A ladder leans against a wall at a $65^\circ$ angle with the ground and touches the wall $12$ ft above the ground. How long is the ladder, in feet, rounded to the nearest tenth?
hint: This time the unknown is the hypotenuse and the known side is opposite the $65^\circ$ angle.

hints.text: This time the unknown is the hypotenuse and the known side is opposite the $65^\circ$ angle.
$\sin 65^\circ = \frac{12}{L}$ — the unknown is downstairs, so multiply both sides by $L$ first.
$L = \frac{12}{\sin 65^\circ} \approx \frac{12}{0.9063} \approx 13.2$ ft.

explanation: The height $12$ ft is opposite the $65^\circ$ angle and the ladder $L$ is the hypotenuse, so use sine.
Write $\sin 65^\circ = \frac{12}{L}$; because $L$ is in the denominator, solve by $L = \frac{12}{\sin 65^\circ}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: The hypotenuse is always biggest
steps: Whatever you compute, the ladder must be longer than the $12$ ft it reaches up the wall.
$13.2 > 12$ ✓. If you had multiplied instead of divided you would have gotten $10.9$ ft — shorter than the wall height, which is impossible.

prompt: Standing $150$ ft from a building, a surveyor whose eyes are $5$ ft above the ground measures the angle of elevation to the roof as $32^\circ$. How tall is the building, in feet, rounded to the nearest tenth?
hint: The triangle starts at eye level, not at the ground — so trigonometry gives only the part of the building ABOVE the surveyor's eyes.

hints.text: The triangle starts at eye level, not at the ground — so trigonometry gives only the part of the building ABOVE the surveyor's eyes.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up without the eye height: standing $100$ ft away at a $45^\circ$ elevation gives $100 \tan 45^\circ = 100$ ft above eye level. Then remember the extra step this problem adds at the end.
Find that upper piece: $\tan 32^\circ = \frac{x}{150}$, so $x = 150 \tan 32^\circ \approx 93.7$ ft.
Add the eye height back: $93.7 + 5 \approx 98.7$ ft.

explanation: The horizontal sight line sits $5$ ft up, so the right triangle has adjacent leg $150$ and opposite leg $x$ = the building above eye level.
The building also extends from the ground up to eye level, so add $5$: about $98.7$ ft tall.

alternativeExplanations.title: Draw the horizontal line first
steps: Sketch the ground, mark the surveyor, and draw a dashed horizontal line from their eyes to the building — that dashed line, not the ground, is the base of the triangle.
The building is then made of two stacked pieces: the $5$ ft below the dashed line and the $93.7$ ft above it.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap answer is $93.7$ ft — a perfectly correct triangle calculation that answers the wrong question. It measures from the surveyor's eyes, not from the ground.
Whenever a problem tells you an eye height, instrument height, or cliff height, it is telling you because it must be added at the end. Circle it in the problem so you do not walk away one step early.

prompt: An accessibility ramp rises $2$ ft over a horizontal run of $24$ ft. Building codes cap the ramp angle at $4.8^\circ$. What angle does this ramp make with the ground, rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree?
hint: Rise is opposite the ramp angle and run is adjacent — that is tangent.

hints.text: Rise is opposite the ramp angle and run is adjacent — that is tangent.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a friendly ratio: a rise of $1$ over a run of $1$ gives $\tan \theta = 1$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}(1) = 45^\circ$. Notice the final move is the inverse tangent, not the ratio itself.
$\tan \theta = \frac{2}{24} \approx 0.0833$. That decimal is the ratio, not the angle.
$\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.0833) \approx 4.8^\circ$, exactly at the legal limit.

explanation: Set up the ratio with the angle at the bottom of the ramp: opposite $= 2$ (rise), adjacent $= 24$ (run).
Undo the tangent: $\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.0833) \approx 4.8^\circ$ — the ramp just barely passes code. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Sanity check with a picture
steps: A ramp that creeps up $2$ ft while stretching $24$ ft forward is nearly flat.
Nearly flat means a tiny angle — a handful of degrees, which points straight at $4.8^\circ$.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice A, $0.1^\circ$, is what you get by reporting $\tan \theta \approx 0.083$ as if it were the angle and rounding — the calculator gave you the RATIO, and you still owe it a $\tan^{-1}$. Choice C, $85.2^\circ$, comes from flipping the fraction to $\frac{24}{2}$, which finds the angle at the TOP of the ramp instead.
Fix both by naming the angle before you compute: stand at the bottom corner, check that the rise is across from you and the run runs away from you, then finish with $\tan^{-1}$.

prompt: In parallelogram $ABCD$, $\angle A = 68^\circ$. What is the measure of $\angle B$, the angle next to it, in degrees?
hint: In a parallelogram, angles that sit next to each other are supplementary — they add to $180^\circ$.

hints.text: In a parallelogram, angles that sit next to each other are supplementary — they add to $180^\circ$.
So $68 + \angle B = 180$.

explanation: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel, so consecutive angles are same-side interior angles and add to $180^\circ$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Check all four
steps: Opposite angles are equal, so the four angles are $68^\circ$, $112^\circ$, $68^\circ$, $112^\circ$.
They total $68 + 112 + 68 + 112 = 360^\circ$ ✓ — exactly what a quadrilateral should have.

prompt: A hexagonal patio tile has $6$ sides. What is the sum of its interior angles, in degrees?
hint: The interior angle sum of an $n$-gon is $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$.

hints.text: The interior angle sum of an $n$-gon is $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Slice it into triangles
steps: Pick one corner of the hexagon and draw diagonals to every non-neighbor corner — you get exactly $4$ triangles.
Every triangle holds $180^\circ$, and together they cover the whole hexagon: $4 \times 180 = 720^\circ$. That is where the $n - 2$ comes from.

prompt: Which statement is true for **every** rectangle but **not** for every rhombus?

choices.label: The diagonals are congruent (equal in length)

hint: Both shapes are parallelograms, so anything true of all parallelograms will be true of both — those cannot be the answer.

hints.text: Both shapes are parallelograms, so anything true of all parallelograms will be true of both — those cannot be the answer.
Picture a long skinny rhombus (a squashed diamond). Are its two diagonals the same length?
No — one is long and one is short. But a rectangle's diagonals are always equal. Choice B.

explanation: A and C are true of every parallelogram, so they do not separate the two shapes.
D is true of every rhombus but false for a non-square rectangle — that is backwards from what the question asks.
B is the winner: rectangles always have congruent diagonals, while a squashed rhombus has one long and one short diagonal.

alternativeExplanations.title: Test with extreme shapes
steps: Imagine a rhombus flattened almost to a line: the diagonals are wildly different lengths.
Now imagine any rectangle: both diagonals stretch corner to corner across the same rectangle, so they must match.

prompt: A clock face is designed as a regular $12$-sided polygon. What is the measure of each exterior angle, in degrees?
hint: The exterior angles of ANY convex polygon always add to $360^\circ$.

hints.text: The exterior angles of ANY convex polygon always add to $360^\circ$.
Regular means all $12$ exterior angles are equal, so divide $360$ by $12$.

explanation: Walking once around any convex polygon turns you through a full $360^\circ$.
In a regular $12$-gon those turns are all equal: $360 \div 12$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Walk the perimeter
steps: Imagine walking along each edge and turning the same amount at every corner.
After $12$ corners you are facing your original direction again, so the $12$ turns total $360^\circ$ — each turn is $30^\circ$.

prompt: A stop sign is a regular octagon ($8$ equal sides and angles). What is the measure of each interior angle, in degrees?
hint: First find the total: $(8 - 2) \times 180$.

hints.text: First find the total: $(8 - 2) \times 180$.
That total is $1080^\circ$, shared equally by $8$ angles.

explanation: Regular means all $8$ angles are equal, so divide by $8$.
Each interior angle of a stop sign is $135^\circ$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Through the exterior angle
steps: Each exterior angle is $360 \div 8 = 45^\circ$.
Interior and exterior angles at a corner form a straight line, so the interior angle is $180 - 45 = 135^\circ$ — same answer, fewer steps.

prompt: Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures $150^\circ$. How many sides does the polygon have?
hint: Going through the exterior angle is far easier than the interior-sum formula.

hints.text: Going through the exterior angle is far easier than the interior-sum formula.
Each exterior angle is $180 - 150 = 30^\circ$, and all the exterior angles add to $360^\circ$.
$360 \div 30 = 12$ sides.

explanation: At each corner, interior + exterior $= 180^\circ$, so each exterior angle is $180 - 150 = 30^\circ$.
The exterior angles of any convex polygon total $360^\circ$.

alternativeExplanations.title: The long way, as a check
steps: If there are $n$ sides, then $\frac{(n - 2) \times 180}{n} = 150$.
Multiply out: $180n - 360 = 150n$, so $30n = 360$ and $n = 12$ ✓ — the same answer the exterior-angle shortcut gave.

prompt: A garden bed is shaped like a trapezoid with parallel sides of $14$ ft and $22$ ft. A hose is laid across the midsegment — the segment joining the midpoints of the two slanted sides. How long is that segment?
hint: The midsegment of a trapezoid is the AVERAGE of the two parallel sides.

hints.text: The midsegment of a trapezoid is the AVERAGE of the two parallel sides.
Average $14$ and $22$: add them, then halve.

explanation: The hose is $18$ ft long. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: It has to land in between
steps: Halfway up the trapezoid, the width must be between $14$ and $22$ — and dead center between them, since it is halfway.
That instantly rules out $8$, $36$, and $11$; only $18$ sits midway.

prompt: In parallelogram $ABCD$, side $\overline{AB}$ has length $3x + 2$ and the opposite side $\overline{CD}$ has length $17$. What is the value of $x$?
hint: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent, so those two expressions are equal.

hints.text: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent, so those two expressions are equal.
Solve $3x + 2 = 17$.

explanation: Opposite sides of a parallelogram have equal length: $3x + 2 = 17$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Geometry sets it up, algebra finishes it
steps: The geometry fact does one job: it turns a picture into the equation $3x + 2 = 17$.
From there it is an ordinary two-step equation — peel off the $+2$, then undo the $\times 3$.

prompt: The interior angles of a polygon add up to $1440^\circ$. How many sides does the polygon have?
hint: Start from $(n - 2) \times 180 = 1440$ and work backwards.

hints.text: Start from $(n - 2) \times 180 = 1440$ and work backwards.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Check the formula on a shape you know: a quadrilateral has $n = 4$, and $(4 - 2) \times 180 = 360^\circ$. ✓ Now run that same equation backwards, starting from $1440$.
Divide both sides by $180$: $n - 2 = 8$.
Add $2$: $n = 10$ sides.

explanation: Set up the interior-angle-sum formula as an equation: $(n - 2) \times 180 = 1440$.
Add $2$ to both sides: $n = 10$. The polygon is a decagon.

alternativeExplanations.title: Count the triangles
steps: $1440 \div 180 = 8$, so the polygon slices into $8$ triangles from one corner.
A polygon always makes two fewer triangles than it has sides, so $8$ triangles means $10$ sides.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap answer is $8$ — you divide $1440 \div 180 = 8$, see a whole number, and stop. But $8$ is the number of TRIANGLES ($n - 2$), not the number of sides.
Write the formula with its parentheses before dividing: $(n - 2) \times 180 = 1440$ makes it obvious that dividing leaves $n - 2$ sitting there, still owed a $+2$.

prompt: A quilt patch is a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other and meet at right angles, but the two diagonals are **not** the same length. What kind of quadrilateral must it be?
hint: Take the clues one at a time. "Diagonals bisect each other" already means the shape is a parallelogram.

hints.text: Take the clues one at a time. "Diagonals bisect each other" already means the shape is a parallelogram.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Sort out an easier case first: a square has diagonals that bisect each other, are perpendicular, AND are equal in length. Your patch matches all of that except equal, so drop whatever the equal length would have added.
Among parallelograms, perpendicular diagonals is the signature of a rhombus; congruent diagonals is the signature of a rectangle.
Perpendicular but NOT congruent means rhombus, and not a square. Choice B.

explanation: Diagonals that bisect each other force a parallelogram, so D is out (a trapezoid is not one).
Perpendicular diagonals make it a rhombus; congruent diagonals would make it a rectangle.
Since the diagonals are perpendicular but unequal, it is a rhombus that is not a square. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Build one and look
steps: Cross a $10$-inch stick and a $6$-inch stick at their midpoints at right angles, then connect the four tips.
All four sides come out equal (each is the hypotenuse of a $5$-$3$ right triangle) but the patch is a stretched diamond, not a square — a rhombus.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap is choosing "square". Perpendicular bisecting diagonals feel square-ish, and a square does fit every clue except the last one — the problem said the diagonals are NOT congruent, and a square's diagonals always are.

When a problem hands you a "not", treat it as an eliminator: read the list of shapes and cross off every one whose diagonals must match. That kills both square and rectangle and leaves rhombus standing.

prompt: A pizza is cut into $8$ equal slices from the center. What is the central angle of one slice, in degrees?
hint: All the way around the center is $360^\circ$.

hints.text: All the way around the center is $360^\circ$.
Eight equal slices share that $360^\circ$ evenly.

explanation: A full circle around the center measures $360^\circ$.
Equal slices means equal central angles: $360 \div 8$.
Each slice has a $45^\circ$ central angle — and its crust is a $45^\circ$ arc.

alternativeExplanations.title: Halve, halve, halve
steps: Cut the pizza in half: $180^\circ$ each. Cut again: $90^\circ$ each.
Cut once more for $8$ slices: $45^\circ$ each.

prompt: A central angle in a circle intercepts an arc of $80^\circ$. An inscribed angle intercepts that same arc. What is the measure of the inscribed angle, in degrees?
hint: An inscribed angle is always half of the arc it intercepts.

hints.text: An inscribed angle is always half of the arc it intercepts.
The arc is $80^\circ$, so take half of it.

explanation: A central angle equals its intercepted arc, so the arc here is $80^\circ$.
An inscribed angle (vertex on the circle) is half its intercepted arc.

alternativeExplanations.title: Center beats edge
steps: Standing at the center, the arc fills your whole field of view: $80^\circ$.
Standing out on the rim, you are farther away and the same arc looks half as wide: $40^\circ$. Vertex at center = full arc, vertex on the circle = half.

prompt: Points $A$ and $B$ are the ends of a diameter of a circle, and $C$ is another point on the circle. What is the measure of $\angle ACB$?
hint: $\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle — its vertex $C$ sits on the circle and it intercepts the arc from $A$ to $B$.

hints.text: $\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle — its vertex $C$ sits on the circle and it intercepts the arc from $A$ to $B$.
Since $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter, the intercepted arc is a semicircle: $180^\circ$.
Half of $180^\circ$ is $90^\circ$ — a right angle, no matter where $C$ sits.

explanation: A diameter splits the circle into two $180^\circ$ arcs.
$\angle ACB$ is inscribed and intercepts one of those semicircular arcs.
Inscribed angle $=$ half the arc $= \frac{180}{2} = 90^\circ$. Choice C.

alternativeExplanations.title: Slide C around and watch
steps: Move $C$ anywhere on the upper half of the circle — near $A$, near $B$, or right on top.
The triangle changes shape completely, but the angle at $C$ stays a perfect right angle every time. That is Thales' theorem.

prompt: A circular garden path has radius $10$ ft. A gardener walks along the arc of a $90^\circ$ section. Write the exact arc length in terms of $\pi$ (for example, write $7\pi$ as 7pi).
hint: Arc length is a fraction of the whole circumference: $\frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$.

hints.text: Arc length is a fraction of the whole circumference: $\frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$.
The whole circumference is $2\pi(10) = 20\pi$, and $90^\circ$ is $\frac{1}{4}$ of the circle.
$\frac{1}{4} \times 20\pi = 5\pi$ ft.

explanation: Circumference of the whole circle: $C = 2\pi r = 20\pi$ ft.
A $90^\circ$ arc is $\frac{90}{360} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the way around.

alternativeExplanations.title: Fraction first, then multiply
steps: Simplify the fraction before touching $\pi$: $\frac{90}{360} = \frac{1}{4}$.
A quarter of $20\pi$ is $5\pi$ — much cleaner than multiplying $20\pi$ by $90$ and dividing by $360$.

prompt: A circular stained-glass window has radius $6$ inches. One colored wedge has a central angle of $120^\circ$. Write the exact area of that wedge in terms of $\pi$ (for example, write $7\pi$ as 7pi).
hint: Sector area is a fraction of the whole circle's area: $\frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$.

hints.text: Sector area is a fraction of the whole circle's area: $\frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$.
Whole circle: $\pi(6)^2 = 36\pi$. And $120^\circ$ is $\frac{1}{3}$ of a full turn.
$\frac{1}{3} \times 36\pi = 12\pi$ square inches.

explanation: Area of the full circle: $\pi r^2 = \pi(6)^2 = 36\pi$ sq in.
$\frac{120}{360} = \frac{1}{3}$, so the wedge is a third of the window.

alternativeExplanations.title: Three wedges make a window
steps: Three $120^\circ$ wedges fit around the center with nothing left over.
So each must be exactly one third of $36\pi$, and $3 \times 12\pi = 36\pi$ ✓

prompt: A circle has radius $13$ cm. A chord of the circle is $24$ cm long. How far is the chord from the center of the circle, in centimeters?
hint: Draw the perpendicular from the center to the chord — it always cuts the chord exactly in half.

hints.text: Draw the perpendicular from the center to the chord — it always cuts the chord exactly in half.
That makes a right triangle with hypotenuse $13$ (a radius) and one leg $24 \div 2 = 12$.

explanation: A radius drawn perpendicular to a chord bisects that chord, so half the chord is $12$ cm.
Connect the center to an endpoint of the chord: that radius is $13$ cm and forms a right triangle with legs $12$ and $d$.
Solve $12^2 + d^2 = 13^2$: $d^2 = 25$, so the chord sits $5$ cm from the center.

alternativeExplanations.title: The 5-12-13 family again
steps: Half-chord $12$, radius $13$ — that is the $5$-$12$-$13$ triple you met in right triangles.
The missing leg is $5$ with no calculation. Circle problems lean on the Pythagorean theorem constantly, so those triples keep paying off.

prompt: A circle has radius $8$ and center $O$. From a point $P$ that is $17$ units from $O$, a tangent line touches the circle at point $T$. How long is $\overline{PT}$?
hint: A radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent line — there is a right angle at $T$.

hints.text: A radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent line — there is a right angle at $T$.
So $\triangle OTP$ is right-angled at $T$, with hypotenuse $OP = 17$ and leg $OT = 8$.

explanation: The tangent meets the radius $\overline{OT}$ at a right angle, so $\triangle OTP$ is a right triangle.
The hypotenuse is $OP = 17$ (it faces the right angle) and one leg is the radius $8$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Which side is the hypotenuse?
steps: The right angle is at $T$, so the side across from it — $\overline{OP}$, the $17$ — is the hypotenuse.
Because the hypotenuse is known, you subtract: $17^2 - 8^2$, landing on the $8$-$15$-$17$ triple.

prompt: A logo has quadrilateral $WXYZ$ with all four vertices on a circle. If $\angle W = 95^\circ$, what is the measure of the opposite angle $\angle Y$, in degrees?
hint: When all four vertices lie on a circle, opposite angles are supplementary.

hints.text: When all four vertices lie on a circle, opposite angles are supplementary.
So $95 + \angle Y = 180$.

explanation: In a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, each pair of opposite angles adds to $180^\circ$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the rule works
steps: $\angle W$ and $\angle Y$ are inscribed angles intercepting the two arcs that together make the whole circle, $360^\circ$.
Each angle is half its arc, so together they are half of $360^\circ$, which is $180^\circ$.

prompt: A lawn sprinkler sprays water $15$ ft in every direction across a $140^\circ$ arc. How many square feet of lawn does it water? Round to the nearest tenth.
hint: The watered patch is a sector: a slice of a circle with radius $15$ ft.

hints.text: The watered patch is a sector: a slice of a circle with radius $15$ ft.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with half a circle: a $180^\circ$ spray of radius $10$ ft covers $\frac{180}{360} \times \pi(10)^2 = 50\pi \approx 157.1$ sq ft. Same fraction-of-a-circle recipe, just with $\frac{140}{360}$ and radius $15$.
Sector area $= \frac{140}{360} \times \pi (15)^2$. Note that $15$ is the radius, since the spray reaches $15$ ft out from the sprinkler.
$\frac{140}{360} \times 225\pi \approx 0.3889 \times 706.86 \approx 274.9$ sq ft.

explanation: The spray distance $15$ ft is the radius, so the full circle would cover $\pi(15)^2 = 225\pi \approx 706.86$ sq ft.
The sprinkler only sweeps $140^\circ$ of that, a fraction of $\frac{140}{360} \approx 0.3889$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Estimate to check
steps: $140^\circ$ is a bit more than a third of a full turn.
A third of $707$ is about $236$, so an answer a little above that — $274.9$ — is believable.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: A common wrong answer is $68.7$ sq ft, from treating $15$ ft as the DIAMETER and using $r = 7.5$. The problem says the water travels $15$ ft outward from the sprinkler, and a distance measured from the center is a radius.
Also watch the other trap: $706.9$, the whole circle, forgetting to take the $\frac{140}{360}$ share. Write the fraction down first, before you ever square the radius.

prompt: A pizza has radius $9$ inches. One slice is cut with a central angle of $40^\circ$. What is the perimeter all the way around that slice — the two straight cuts plus the curved crust — in inches, rounded to the nearest tenth?
hint: Walk around the slice: out along one cut, along the crust, back along the other cut. That is three pieces.

hints.text: Walk around the slice: out along one cut, along the crust, back along the other cut. That is three pieces.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a half pizza of radius $2$: the two straight cuts total $4$, and the crust is $\frac{180}{360} \times 2\pi(2) = 2\pi \approx 6.3$, for about $10.3$ in. Two radii plus the arc, every time.
The two straight cuts are radii: $9 + 9 = 18$ in. The crust is an arc: $\frac{40}{360} \times 2\pi(9)$.
Arc $= \frac{1}{9} \times 18\pi = 2\pi \approx 6.3$ in, so the perimeter is $18 + 6.3 = 24.3$ in.

explanation: The two straight edges of the slice are radii, contributing $9 + 9 = 18$ inches.
The crust is a $40^\circ$ arc: $\frac{40}{360} \times 2\pi(9) = \frac{1}{9}(18\pi) = 2\pi \approx 6.28$ inches.

alternativeExplanations.title: Trace it with your finger
steps: Start at the pizza's center, slide out $9$ in to the crust, curve $6.3$ in along the edge, then slide $9$ in back to the center.
Add the three legs of that trip: $9 + 6.3 + 9 = 24.3$ inches.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice A, $6.3$, is the arc alone — the answer of someone who read "perimeter" but computed only the crust. Choice B, $18.0$, is the opposite mistake: the straight cuts with no crust.
Perimeter means the ENTIRE boundary. Before computing, trace the outline with your finger and count how many separate pieces you crossed; here there are three, so your sum needs three terms.

prompt: A triangular flag has a base of $14$ inches and a height of $9$ inches. What is its area, in square inches?
hint: Area of a triangle is $\frac{1}{2}bh$.

hints.text: Area of a triangle is $\frac{1}{2}bh$.
$14 \times 9 = 126$. Now take half.
$\frac{1}{2}(126) = 63$ square inches.

explanation: Halve it: the flag covers $63$ square inches.

alternativeExplanations.title: Half of a rectangle
steps: A $14$-by-$9$ rectangle has area $126$ sq in.
Any triangle with that same base and height is exactly half of it — cut the rectangle along a diagonal and see. So $63$ sq in.

prompt: A parallelogram-shaped tile has a base of $12$ cm and a height of $7$ cm. What is its area, in square centimeters?
hint: Area of a parallelogram is base times height — no halving.

hints.text: Area of a parallelogram is base times height — no halving.
Multiply $12 \times 7$.
$12 \times 7 = 84$ square centimeters.

alternativeExplanations.title: Slide the triangle over
steps: Cut the slanted triangle off one end of the parallelogram and slide it to the other end.
You now have a $12$-by-$7$ rectangle with the same area: $84$ sq cm. That is why the formula matches a rectangle's.

prompt: A round mirror has a radius of $5$ inches. What is its exact area?
hint: Area of a circle is $\pi r^2$ — the radius gets squared, not doubled.

hints.text: Area of a circle is $\pi r^2$ — the radius gets squared, not doubled.
$5^2 = 25$, so the area is $25\pi$ square inches. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Sort the two formulas
steps: $2\pi r$ is CIRCUMFERENCE — a distance around, measured in inches. With $r = 5$ that is the $10\pi$ in choice A.
$\pi r^2$ is AREA — a covering, measured in square inches. The question asks for area, so square the radius: $25\pi$.

prompt: A trapezoid-shaped flower bed has parallel sides of $6$ ft and $10$ ft, and the distance between those parallel sides is $5$ ft. What is its area, in square feet?
hint: Trapezoid area is $\frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h$ — average the two parallel sides, then multiply by the height.

hints.text: Trapezoid area is $\frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h$ — average the two parallel sides, then multiply by the height.
Average: $\frac{6 + 10}{2} = 8$. Now multiply by the height $5$.
$8 \times 5 = 40$ square feet.

explanation: Half of that is the average width: $8$ ft.
Multiply by the height: $8 \times 5 = 40$ square feet.

alternativeExplanations.title: A rectangle in disguise
steps: A trapezoid is a rectangle whose top has been widened at one end and narrowed at the other.
On average it is $8$ ft wide and it is $5$ ft deep, so it holds the same area as an $8$-by-$5$ rectangle: $40$ sq ft.

prompt: A garden bed is L-shaped: start with a rectangle $10$ ft long and $6$ ft wide, then cut away a $4$ ft by $3$ ft rectangle from one corner. What is the area of the remaining L-shaped bed, in square feet?
hint: Find the big rectangle's area, then subtract the piece that was removed.

hints.text: Find the big rectangle's area, then subtract the piece that was removed.
Big rectangle: $10 \times 6 = 60$ sq ft. Removed corner: $4 \times 3 = 12$ sq ft.
$60 - 12 = 48$ square feet.

explanation: Treat the L as a full rectangle with a bite taken out.
Full rectangle: $10 \times 6 = 60$ sq ft. Bite: $4 \times 3 = 12$ sq ft.

alternativeExplanations.title: Add two pieces instead
steps: You can also slice the L into two rectangles: one $10$ by $3$ ($30$ sq ft) and one $6$ by $3$ ($18$ sq ft).
$30 + 18 = 48$ sq ft ✓ — subtracting a piece and adding pieces always agree, so use whichever cut you see first.

prompt: A regular pentagon tabletop has sides of $8$ inches and an apothem (the distance from the center to the middle of a side) of $5.5$ inches. What is its area, in square inches?
hint: For a regular polygon, $A = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{perimeter} \times \text{apothem}$.

hints.text: For a regular polygon, $A = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{perimeter} \times \text{apothem}$.
Perimeter $= 5 \times 8 = 40$ inches.
$A = \frac{1}{2}(40)(5.5) = 20 \times 5.5 = 110$ square inches.

explanation: Find the perimeter first: five sides of $8$ in give $P = 40$ in.

alternativeExplanations.title: Five triangles from the center
steps: Draw segments from the center to each corner: the pentagon becomes $5$ identical triangles, each with base $8$ and height $5.5$ (the apothem).
One triangle is $\frac{1}{2}(8)(5.5) = 22$ sq in, and $5 \times 22 = 110$ sq in. That is exactly what the $\frac{1}{2}Pa$ formula packages up.

hint: Unprinted area $=$ square area $-$ circle area.

hints.text: Unprinted area $=$ square area $-$ circle area.
The square is $10 \times 10 = 100$. The circle has diameter $10$, so its radius is $5$ and its area is $25\pi$.

explanation: The circle touches all four sides, so its diameter is $10$ and its radius is $5$: area $= \pi(5)^2 = 25\pi \approx 78.5$ sq cm.
Subtract: $100 - 78.5 = 21.5$ sq cm in the four corners. Choice A.

alternativeExplanations.title: Eyeball the corners
steps: The circle nearly fills the napkin, leaving only four small corner scraps.
Those scraps should be a small slice of the $100$ sq cm total — around a fifth — so $21.5$ fits and $78.5$ (choice C, the circle itself) clearly does not.

prompt: A round pizza has a diameter of $14$ inches. Using $\pi \approx 3.14$, what is its area in square inches, rounded to the nearest whole number?
hint: The formula needs the radius, but you were handed the diameter.

hints.text: The formula needs the radius, but you were handed the diameter.
Radius $= 14 \div 2 = 7$ inches. Now use $A = \pi r^2$.
$A \approx 3.14 \times 49 \approx 153.86 \approx 154$ square inches.

explanation: Halve the diameter to get the radius: $r = 7$ inches.
Multiply by $\pi$: $3.14 \times 49 = 153.86$, which rounds to $154$ square inches.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the halving matters so much
steps: Skipping the halving means using $r = 14$, giving $3.14 \times 196 \approx 615$ sq in — four times too big.
Squaring doubles every mistake: a radius that is twice too large makes an area four times too large. Circle the word "diameter" the moment you read it.

prompt: A stained-glass window is a $3$ ft wide by $4$ ft tall rectangle with a semicircle sitting on top of it, so the semicircle's diameter is the $3$ ft top edge. What is the total area of the window, in square feet, rounded to the nearest hundredth?
hint: Split the window into two shapes you already know: a rectangle plus a half circle.

hints.text: Split the window into two shapes you already know: a rectangle plus a half circle.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Start with just the rectangle: $3 \times 4 = 12$ sq ft, which would be the whole answer if the top edge were flat. The semicircle only adds a piece, and its radius is half of that $3$ ft edge.
Rectangle: $3 \times 4 = 12$ sq ft. The semicircle has DIAMETER $3$, so its radius is $1.5$.
Semicircle $= \frac{1}{2}\pi(1.5)^2 \approx 3.53$ sq ft, so the total is $12 + 3.53 = 15.53$ sq ft.

explanation: The semicircle spans the $3$ ft top edge, so that $3$ ft is the diameter and the radius is $1.5$ ft.
Semicircle piece: $\frac{1}{2}\pi(1.5)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\pi(2.25) \approx 3.53$ sq ft. Total: $12 + 3.53 = 15.53$ square feet.

alternativeExplanations.title: Estimate the top piece
steps: The arch is a half circle about $3$ ft across and $1.5$ ft tall, so it should cover a few square feet at most.
$3.53$ sq ft fits that picture, and adding it to the $12$ sq ft rectangle gives roughly $15.5$ sq ft of glass.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The classic wrong answer is $26.14$: using $r = 3$ for the semicircle because the number $3$ was printed on the drawing. But $3$ ft is the width the arch spans, which is a diameter, not a radius.
Say it out loud as you work: "the arch sits ON the $3$ ft edge, so $3$ is the diameter, so $r = 1.5$." Then halve the circle area exactly once, at the end.

prompt: A square patio tile is $12$ in on each side. A quarter circle with radius $12$ in is drawn with its center at one corner of the tile, and that quarter circle is painted blue. How many square inches of the tile stay unpainted? Round to the nearest tenth.
hint: Unpainted $=$ square $-$ quarter circle.

hints.text: Unpainted $=$ square $-$ quarter circle.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try smaller: a $2$ by $2$ square with a quarter circle of radius $2$ leaves $4 - \frac{1}{4}\pi(2)^2 = 4 - \pi \approx 0.9$ sq in unpainted. Same subtraction, bigger numbers.
Square: $12^2 = 144$ sq in. Quarter circle: $\frac{1}{4}\pi(12)^2 = 36\pi$.

explanation: The whole tile is $12 \times 12 = 144$ square inches.
The blue region is one quarter of a circle of radius $12$: $\frac{1}{4}\pi(12)^2 = \frac{1}{4}(144\pi) = 36\pi \approx 113.1$ sq in.

alternativeExplanations.title: Sensible-size check
steps: A quarter circle of radius $12$ drawn from a corner of a $12$-inch square fills most of the tile, leaving only the far corner region.
So the leftover must be well under half of $144$ — about $31$ sq in, roughly a fifth of the tile.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice C, $113.1$, is the painted quarter circle itself — a correct calculation of the wrong region, since the question asks for what is left UNPAINTED. Choice B comes from taking a quarter of the radius instead of a quarter of the area.
Underline what the question asks for before computing, and finish by asking "did I subtract?" Here the last move must be $144 - 113.1$.

prompt: A moving box is a rectangular prism measuring $3$ ft by $4$ ft by $5$ ft. What is its volume, in cubic feet?
hint: Volume of a rectangular prism is length $\times$ width $\times$ height.

hints.text: Volume of a rectangular prism is length $\times$ width $\times$ height.
$3 \times 4 = 12$. Now multiply by $5$.
$12 \times 5 = 60$ cubic feet.

alternativeExplanations.title: Layers of cubes
steps: The bottom layer is a $3$-by-$4$ grid: $12$ one-foot cubes.
The box is $5$ ft tall, so it holds $5$ of those layers: $5 \times 12 = 60$ cubes.

prompt: A cylindrical can has radius $3$ in and height $10$ in. Write its exact volume in terms of $\pi$ (for example, write $7\pi$ as 7pi).
hint: A cylinder is a stack of identical circles: $V = \pi r^2 h$.

hints.text: A cylinder is a stack of identical circles: $V = \pi r^2 h$.
The circular base has area $\pi(3)^2 = 9\pi$ square inches.
Multiply by the height: $9\pi \times 10 = 90\pi$ cubic inches.

explanation: Volume is base area times height: $9\pi \times 10$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Base times height, always
steps: Every prism and cylinder follows the same rule: area of the base, times how tall it is.
For a box the base is a rectangle; for a can it is a circle. Same idea, different base formula.

prompt: A gift box is a cube with edges of $4$ inches. How much wrapping paper covers its outside exactly, with no overlap?
hint: A cube has $6$ identical square faces.

hints.text: A cube has $6$ identical square faces.
Each face is $4 \times 4 = 16$ sq in.
$6 \times 16 = 96$ square inches. Choice D.

explanation: Surface area counts every face: a cube has $6$ of them.

alternativeExplanations.title: Sort out the near misses
steps: $16$ is one face only; $24$ comes from $6 \times 4$, multiplying the six faces by the EDGE instead of by the face area; and $64$ is the VOLUME, $4^3$ — what fits inside, not what covers it.
Wrapping paper is a covering, so it is measured in square inches and needs all six faces: $96$.

prompt: An ice-cream cone has radius $3$ in and height $8$ in. Write the exact volume of the cone in terms of $\pi$ (for example, write $7\pi$ as 7pi).
hint: A cone is exactly one third of the cylinder that surrounds it: $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$.

hints.text: A cone is exactly one third of the cylinder that surrounds it: $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$.
The matching cylinder holds $\pi(3)^2(8) = 72\pi$.
One third of $72\pi$ is $24\pi$ cubic inches.

alternativeExplanations.title: Three cones fill one cylinder
steps: If you fill a cone with water and pour it into a cylinder of the same radius and height, it takes exactly three cone-fulls to fill it.
That is where the $\frac{1}{3}$ comes from — and it also appears in the pyramid formula for the same reason.

prompt: A spherical exercise ball has radius $6$ inches. Write its exact volume in terms of $\pi$ (for example, write $7\pi$ as 7pi).
hint: Sphere volume is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ — the radius is CUBED.

hints.text: Sphere volume is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ — the radius is CUBED.
$\frac{4}{3}(216) = 288$, so $V = 288\pi$ cubic inches.

alternativeExplanations.title: Divide before you multiply
steps: $\frac{4}{3} \times 216$ is easiest as $216 \div 3 = 72$, then $72 \times 4 = 288$.
Dividing first keeps the numbers small and avoids a messy $864 \div 3$.

prompt: A cylindrical water tank has radius $4$ ft and height $10$ ft. What is its volume in cubic feet, rounded to the nearest whole number?
hint: Use $V = \pi r^2 h$ and keep $\pi$ until the end.

hints.text: Use $V = \pi r^2 h$ and keep $\pi$ until the end.
$\pi(4)^2(10) = 160\pi$ cubic feet.
$160\pi \approx 502.65$, which rounds to $503$ cubic feet.

explanation: $160 \times 3.14159 \approx 502.65$, so the tank holds about $503$ cubic feet.

alternativeExplanations.title: Rough check in your head
steps: $\pi$ is a little more than $3$, so $160\pi$ is a little more than $480$.
$503$ sits just above that estimate ✓ — a good sign you squared the radius and did not square the height.

prompt: A model cube is rebuilt with every edge $3$ times as long. The surface area of the new cube is how many times the surface area of the original?
hint: Surface area is built from two dimensions, so scaling hits it twice.

hints.text: Surface area is built from two dimensions, so scaling hits it twice.
Test it: a cube of edge $1$ has surface area $6$; a cube of edge $3$ has surface area $6(3^2) = 54$.
$54 \div 6 = 9$ times as much.

explanation: If every length is multiplied by $k$, area is multiplied by $k^2$ and volume by $k^3$.
Here $k = 3$, so surface area grows by $3^2 = 9$.
The new cube has $9$ times the surface area (and $27$ times the volume).

alternativeExplanations.title: Look at one face
steps: One face goes from a $1$-by-$1$ square to a $3$-by-$3$ square — that is $9$ little squares instead of $1$.
All six faces grow the same way, so the whole surface is $9$ times bigger.

prompt: A glass paperweight is a pyramid with a square base $6$ cm on each side and a height of $10$ cm. What is its volume?
hint: Pyramid volume is $\frac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times \text{height}$.

hints.text: Pyramid volume is $\frac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times \text{height}$.
Base area $= 6 \times 6 = 36$ sq cm, and $36 \times 10 = 360$.
Take a third: $360 \div 3 = 120$ cubic cm. Choice B.

explanation: The base is a square: $6^2 = 36$ square centimeters.
A box with that base and height $10$ would hold $360$ cubic cm.
A pyramid holds one third of that: $V = 120$ cubic centimeters. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why choice D is so tempting
steps: $360$ is the volume of the BOX around the pyramid — what you get by forgetting the $\frac{1}{3}$.
A pyramid tapers to a point, so it obviously holds less than the box it fits inside. Any pointed solid (cone or pyramid) carries that $\frac{1}{3}$.

prompt: An ice-cream treat is a cone of radius $3$ in and height $10$ in, topped by a perfect hemisphere (half a ball) of ice cream with radius $3$ in. Write the exact total volume in terms of $\pi$ (for example, write $7\pi$ as 7pi).
hint: Two solids, two formulas, then add: cone $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$ and hemisphere (half of $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$).

hints.text: Two solids, two formulas, then add: cone $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$ and hemisphere (half of $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$).

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Do one solid at a time: a cone of radius $3$ and height $1$ alone holds $\frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(1) = 3\pi$. Once that step feels routine, redo it with height $10$ and then add the hemisphere.
Cone: $\frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(10) = 30\pi$. Hemisphere: $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3}\pi(27) = 18\pi$.
$30\pi + 18\pi = 48\pi$ cubic inches.

explanation: Hemisphere: a full sphere is $\frac{4}{3}\pi(3)^3 = 36\pi$, and half of that is $18\pi$ cubic inches.
Add the two pieces: $30\pi + 18\pi = 48\pi$ cubic inches (about $150.8$).

alternativeExplanations.title: Handle one solid at a time
steps: Write "cone $=$" and "hemisphere $=$" on two separate lines before computing anything — composite solids go wrong when the work gets tangled.
Both pieces here share the same radius $3$, but only the cone uses the height $10$; the hemisphere is governed entirely by its radius.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The usual wrong answer is $66\pi$: using the FULL sphere formula, $36\pi$, instead of halving it for a hemisphere.

The word "hemisphere" means half a ball, so compute the sphere and then cut it in two: $36\pi \to 18\pi$. A quick check: the scoop on top should be smaller than the tall cone below it, and $18\pi < 30\pi$ ✓

prompt: Two cylindrical soup cans are similar (the same shape, different sizes). The small can is $3$ in tall and the large can is $5$ in tall. What is the ratio of the small can's volume to the large can's volume?
hint: For similar solids: lengths scale by $k$, surface areas by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$.

hints.text: For similar solids: lengths scale by $k$, surface areas by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: See it on cubes: a $1$ by $1$ by $1$ cube holds $1$ and a $2$ by $2$ by $2$ cube holds $8$ — lengths $1 : 2$ but volumes $1 : 8$, the ratio cubed. Do the same cubing to $3 : 5$.
Here $k = \frac{3}{5}$, and volume needs the cube.
$\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3 = \frac{27}{125}$, so the ratio is $27 : 125$. Choice C.

explanation: Similar solids have all matching lengths in the same ratio, here $3 : 5$.
Volume is a three-dimensional measure, so it scales by the cube of that ratio.

alternativeExplanations.title: Check it with real numbers
steps: Say the small can has radius $3$ and height $3$: $V = \pi(9)(3) = 27\pi$.
The similar large can has radius $5$ and height $5$: $V = \pi(25)(5) = 125\pi$. The ratio is $27\pi : 125\pi = 27 : 125$ ✓

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice A, $3 : 5$, is the trap: assuming volume scales the same way length does. It does not — the large can is not merely $\frac{5}{3}$ as roomy, it is more than four times as roomy.
Ask what KIND of measure the question wants: a length uses $k$, an area (paint, labels, wrapping) uses $k^2$, a volume (soup, water, sand) uses $k^3$. Soup fills space, so cube it.

prompt: A game piece sits at $(2, 5)$. It is translated $3$ units right and $4$ units down. Write its new coordinates in the form (x, y).
hint: Right changes only $x$; down changes only $y$.

hints.text: Right changes only $x$; down changes only $y$.
The piece lands at $(5, 1)$.

explanation: A translation slides a point without turning or resizing it.
Moving right adds to $x$: $2 + 3 = 5$. Moving down subtracts from $y$: $5 - 4 = 1$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Walk it on the grid
steps: Start at $(2, 5)$ and take three steps right — you are at $(5, 5)$.
Now take four steps down to $(5, 1)$. Same answer, no formula needed.

prompt: The point $(4, -3)$ is reflected across the $x$-axis. Write the coordinates of the image in the form (x, y).
hint: The $x$-axis is a horizontal mirror, so the point flips up or down but never sideways.

hints.text: The $x$-axis is a horizontal mirror, so the point flips up or down but never sideways.
Keep $x$ the same and change the sign of $y$: $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$.

explanation: Reflecting across the $x$-axis leaves the horizontal position alone and flips the vertical one.
So $(4, -3) \to (4, 3)$ — it was $3$ below the axis, now it is $3$ above.

alternativeExplanations.title: Mirror distance check
steps: The point was $3$ units below the $x$-axis.
A mirror image sits the same distance on the other side, so it must be $3$ units above, still in the same column $x = 4$: $(4, 3)$.

hints.text: The rule for $90^\circ$ counterclockwise is $(x, y) \to (-y, x)$: swap, then negate the new first coordinate.
With $(3, 1)$: swap to get $(1, 3)$, then negate the first: $(-1, 3)$.
The image is $(-1, 3)$. Choice A.

explanation: A $90^\circ$ counterclockwise turn about the origin follows $(x, y) \to (-y, x)$.
Here $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, so the image is $(-1, 3)$.
Choice A. (Choice B is the clockwise rotation and choice C is a $180^\circ$ turn.)

alternativeExplanations.title: Which quadrant should it land in?
steps: $(3, 1)$ sits in Quadrant I, just above the positive $x$-axis.
Turning counterclockwise a quarter turn carries Quadrant I into Quadrant II, where $x$ is negative and $y$ is positive — only $(-1, 3)$ qualifies.

hints.text: Perpendicular slopes are opposite reciprocals: flip the fraction and change the sign.
Flip $\frac{2}{3}$ to get $\frac{3}{2}$.

explanation: Two lines are perpendicular exactly when their slopes multiply to $-1$.
Flip $\frac{2}{3}$ upside down to get $\frac{3}{2}$, then negate it: $-\frac{3}{2}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: See it as a turn
steps: Slope $\frac{2}{3}$ means "over $3$, up $2$" — a gentle uphill.
Rotate that step a quarter turn and it becomes "over $2$, down $3$", which is slope $-\frac{3}{2}$: steeper, and heading downhill.
